rows.stem:
f is a continuous function defined for all real x, with f(0) = 2. The sign of f'(x) and f''(x) are given below.

| Interval | f'(x) | f''(x) |
|---|---|---|
| x < 1 | positive | negative |
| 1 < x < 2 | negative | negative |
| 2 < x < 3 | negative | positive |
| x > 3 | positive | positive |

Write the item ID HDG-2026-CALCAB-001 at the top of your page. Sketch a possible graph of f(x) for -1 <= x <= 5 that is consistent with this table and with f(0) = 2.
rows.capture_instruction: Draw one graph on one page. Write only the item ID at the top of the page, then photograph the full page with all graph evidence visible.
rows.canonical_answer: The curve increases and is concave down for x < 1, reaching a local maximum at x = 1 (horizontal tangent, since f' changes from positive to negative). It then decreases from x = 1 to x = 3, remaining concave down until x = 2 and then switching to concave up from x = 2 to x = 3 (an inflection point at x = 2, visible as a change in curvature while the curve is still falling). At x = 3 the curve reaches a local minimum (horizontal tangent, since f' changes from negative to positive) and then increases and is concave up for x > 3. The curve passes through the point (0, 2).

expected_graph_spec.representation: single smooth curve, f(x) vs. x
expected_graph_spec.y_axis: f(x), any consistent scale passing through (0, 2)
accepted_variants: exact y-values other than f(0)=2 are not graded -- only the shape (monotonicity, extrema locations, concavity, inflection location) must match

criterion_definitions.met_rule: The curve is rising (increasing) for all x < 1.
The curve has a local maximum (horizontal tangent / turning point from rising to falling) at x = 1.
The curve is falling (decreasing) continuously from x = 1 to x = 3.
The curve has a local minimum (horizontal tangent / turning point from falling to rising) at x = 3.
The curve is rising (increasing) for all x > 3.
A visible change in concavity (from concave down to concave up) occurs at x = 2, while the curve is still decreasing on both sides of it.
The curve is concave down for x < 1 (bending toward the local max at x = 1).
The curve passes through or very near the point (0, 2).

rows.stem:
f is a smooth, differentiable function for -2 <= x <= 4 with the following behavior: f is decreasing on (-2, 0), has a relative minimum at x = 0, is increasing on (0, 2), has a relative maximum at x = 2, and is decreasing on (2, 4). f has no other critical points on this interval.

Write the item ID HDG-2026-CALCAB-002 at the top of your page. Sketch the graph of f'(x) for -2 <= x <= 4, using the behavior of f described above. You do not need to find a formula for f or f'.
rows.capture_instruction: Draw one graph on one page. Write only the item ID at the top of the page, then photograph the full page with all graph evidence visible.
rows.canonical_answer: Since f is decreasing on (-2, 0), f'(x) < 0 there. Since f has a relative minimum at x = 0, f'(0) = 0 and f' changes from negative to positive there. Since f is increasing on (0, 2), f'(x) > 0 there. Since f has a relative maximum at x = 2, f'(2) = 0 and f' changes from positive to negative there. Since f is decreasing on (2, 4), f'(x) < 0 there. The sketch of f' is therefore a curve that is negative on (-2, 0), crosses zero (going upward) at x = 0, positive on (0, 2), crosses zero (going downward) at x = 2, and negative on (2, 4) -- with no other zero crossings on the interval.

expected_graph_spec.y_axis: f'(x), any consistent scale showing the correct sign in each region
accepted_variants: exact curve shape between zeros is not graded -- only the sign of f' in each interval and the location/direction of the two zero crossings must match

criterion_definitions.met_rule: f' is drawn below the x-axis (negative) for all x in (-2, 0).
f' crosses the x-axis at x = 0, going from negative to positive (upward crossing).
f' is drawn above the x-axis (positive) for all x in (0, 2).
f' crosses the x-axis at x = 2, going from positive to negative (downward crossing).
f' is drawn below the x-axis (negative) for all x in (2, 4).
f' does not cross the x-axis anywhere else on (-2, 4) besides x = 0 and x = 2.
The horizontal axis is labeled x and the vertical axis is labeled f'(x), spanning at least -2 to 4.
